# HA authority audit

Generated by `hack/cnpatroni/audit` from `policy/authority-rules.yaml`, the classification file beside it, and the
tree as it stands. The document carries no build stamp on purpose: a timestamp or a commit hash would
change on every commit and turn the drift check into noise, so this file changes only when the audit
actually changes. Provenance for the numbers is the baseline record below.

This is the audit required by specification section 9.1. It inventories every reachable code path in
this repository that can influence PostgreSQL role or process lifecycle, and records what
CloudNativePatroni intends to do about each one.

## How this document is maintained

This file is generated. Editing it by hand is pointless: the next `doc` run overwrites it, and the
continuous-integration job fails when the committed copy differs from a fresh render.

The judgement a scanner cannot produce, which is what to do about a symbol, lives in
`hack/cnpatroni/audit/policy/authority-classification.yaml`. The scanner cross-checks that file in
both directions: every hit it finds must be classified, and every classification must still name a
symbol that exists. A code path that appears during an upstream merge and has no classification
fails the check by name, which is the mechanism specification section 9.3 asks for.

The prose in the fork-feasibility section below is a template fragment,
`hack/cnpatroni/audit/policy/authority-audit-narrative.md`, into which the measured numbers are
substituted at render time. Two numbers in that section are exceptions, because they describe git
history rather than the current tree; they are marked as hand-measured and carry the command that
produced them.

### Forbidden-call baseline

The baseline is the ratchet. On day one this repository is unmodified CloudNativePG and is full of
forbidden calls, so a gate that failed on any of them would be red from the first commit and would be
switched off within a week. The recorded totals may fall and must never rise.

Recorded from commit `b22682115c5f3ad1bfe69bed719151d0db918e39` at 2026-08-10 00:12:54 UTC.

| Measure | Value |
|---|---:|
| Forbidden hits recorded | 113 |
| Buckets, keyed by rule and enclosing symbol | 88 |

Buckets are keyed by `(rule, enclosing symbol)` rather than by file and line. Line numbers churn on
every upstream merge, and a file-keyed baseline would let a merge add a brand new forbidden call
inside a file that is already listed. A new function is always a new bucket, so that case fails.

## Fork feasibility

This section answers owner directive D-5. The decision to adopt Patroni is settled and this audit does
not reopen it. What the audit has to establish is whether the fork is feasible on the terms the
specification assumes: that the authority is concentrated, that the entangled non-HA machinery which
must relocate is a bounded amount of work, and that the resulting diff stays concentrated enough for
upstream integration to remain affordable.

Every number below is substituted from the scan at render time. The two measurements the scanner
cannot take, both about upstream churn, are marked as such and carry their command.

### The finding, in three sentences

CloudNativePG's high-availability authority is concentrated: 119 forbidden hits sit in
84 functions across 39 files and 23 packages,
of which `github.com/cloudnative-pg/cloudnative-pg/pkg/management/postgres` alone accounts for 39 per cent and the three
largest packages together account for 68 per cent. The entangled non-HA machinery is
a bounded relocation rather than a rewrite: of the 22 instance-manager
responsibilities, the ones that keep a home are a handful of in-database reconcilers, credential
rotation, metrics, logs and the backup endpoints, and their only shared change is that each must ask
Patroni which instance is the leader instead of reading the CloudNativePG cluster status. The fork is feasible on the specification's terms, with one
qualification that has to be stated rather than smoothed over: the diff is concentrated by package
but not by file, because the largest single site,
`pkg/management/postgres/instance.go`, is also a file upstream edits regularly, so the ongoing
integration cost is dominated by a small number of hot files rather than spread thinly.

### 1. How concentrated is the authority

| Measure | Value |
|---|---:|
| Forbidden hits | 119 |
| Functions containing them | 84 |
| Files containing them | 39 |
| Packages containing them | 23 |
| Go files inspected in total | 568 |
| Share of forbidden hits in `github.com/cloudnative-pg/cloudnative-pg/pkg/management/postgres` | 39 per cent |
| Share of forbidden hits in the three largest packages | 68 per cent |
| Recorded in the baseline after the allowlist | 113 |
| Baseline buckets, keyed by rule and symbol | 88 |

39 files out of 568 inspected carry the authority that has to become
unreachable. That is the number the specification's assumption rests on, and it holds.

The call-graph shape matters as much as the count. The forbidden primitives are reached through few
entry points: promotion has exactly one caller, the postmaster exec has exactly one caller, and the
single operator-side writer of the desired-primary field is one function. Milestone M1 therefore has
a small number of cut points rather than a diffuse edit, which is what makes the runtime guard a
practical mechanism rather than a gesture.

Two authority paths were found that the specification's own high-risk file list in section 9.2 does
not name, and both would have been left live by a change that followed that list literally:

- the Lease renewal, take-over and preemption logic lives in
  `internal/cmd/manager/instance/run/lease`, not in `internal/controller/primary_lease.go`, which
  only creates the Lease object. The preemption branch shuts the manager down and stops PostgreSQL;
- the promotion-candidate selector is a `sort.Interface` implementation,
  `(*PostgresqlStatusList).Less`, whose caller takes the first element. A selection rule hidden in a
  sort is exactly what an upstream merge reintroduces without anyone noticing.

Both are classified here, which is the point of running the scan rather than transcribing the list.

### 2. What must relocate, and how much of it there is

Two tables are needed here, and reading only the first would mislead. The classification counts
describe the symbols the scanner surfaced, and the scanner surfaces authority paths by construction,
so that table is heavily weighted towards "disable" and says nothing about how much safe machinery
has to move. The responsibility destinations are the honest measure of relocation volume.

| Class | Symbols |
|---|---:|
| disable | 86 |
| adapt | 22 |
| move | 1 |
| keep | 0 |
| delete-later | 3 |

| Destination | Classified symbols | Responsibilities |
|---|---:|---:|
| disabled | 89 | 13 |
| operator | 12 | 2 |
| cnpatroni-agent | 8 | 4 |
| Patroni container | 2 | 1 |
| finite init | 1 | 2 |

The relocation work is real but bounded. The instance manager holds
22 distinct responsibilities in
[the responsibility map](responsibility-map.md); the ones that have to move rather than disappear are
the declarative in-database reconcilers, credential rotation, the metrics exporter, the log pipes and
the backup remote procedure calls, all of which are ordinary SQL and file work with no process
authority. Their only common change is that each one currently asks the CloudNativePG cluster status
which instance is the primary, and each must instead ask Patroni. That is one substitution applied in
several places, not several designs.

Two pieces of relocation are harder than the rest and should be planned as such: the filesystem
preparation that currently runs inside the long-lived instance manager has to become a finite init
that exits, and the replication and rewind users have to be created where Patroni can find them.
Neither is architecturally novel; both are places where getting the ordering wrong produces a
cluster that starts and then fails later.

### 3. Does the diff stay concentrated

By package, yes: 68 per cent of the forbidden hits are in three packages, and
23 packages hold all of them. Classified symbols touch
50 files in 26 directories.

By file, the answer needs a caveat. The concentration is achieved partly because
`pkg/management/postgres/instance.go` is a large file that holds many primitives at once, and a large
frequently-edited file is the worst place for a fork's diff to live: every upstream change to it is a
potential conflict, whether or not it touches the parts we changed.

The two churn measurements below were taken by hand on 2026-08-10, because they are statements about
git history rather than about the current tree, and the scanner deliberately does not read history:

```bash
git log --name-only --format= HEAD~48..HEAD | grep '\.go$' | sort -u | wc -l
```

Over the 48 upstream commits available in this clone, 105 Go files were modified, and 9 of the
39 files carrying forbidden hits were among them. The measurement is bounded: this
is a shallow clone, so 48 commits is roughly a fortnight of upstream activity and not a release
cycle. It should be repeated against a full clone before the M1 plan is fixed, and the result
recorded here. Taken at face value it says that roughly a quarter of the files the fork must change
are also files upstream touches within any two-week window, which is the number that predicts the
long-term integration cost.

The mitigation the specification already provides is the right one, and this audit is part of it:
the surgery is expressed as small, local cuts at named symbols, each guarded and each recorded here,
rather than as a restructuring of the files that hold them. A cut of a few lines inside a hot file
conflicts far less often than a reorganisation of the same file.

### What this finding does not claim

It does not claim that the audit proves the authority is gone. A static analysis cannot see through
reflection or through an interface whose implementation is chosen at run time, which is why the
specification places the real proof in the M3 chaos suite. It does not claim anything about Patroni's
own behaviour, which is upstream's and outside this repository. And it does not claim that a
concentrated diff makes upstream integration cheap; it makes it affordable, and the churn measurement
above is the number to watch.

## Instance-manager responsibility map

The second requirement of specification section 9.1, which is a statement about responsibilities
rather than about symbols, is rendered separately as
[the responsibility map](responsibility-map.md). It is generated from the same data file and is
anchored on real symbols, so an upstream change that deletes an anchor flags the responsibility row
as stale.

## The container startup contract, and why it has no test yet

Design B pairs this audit with a third guardrail: a check that the database container's startup path
cannot become a supervisor. That guardrail is **not implemented in M0**, and the reason is worth
stating plainly rather than hiding behind a green tick.

There is nothing to inspect. This repository contains no entrypoint script, no image directory, and
no database-image Dockerfile; the only `Dockerfile` present builds the operator and its entry point is
already exec form. A checker written against those files today would assert nothing and would report
success, which is worse than no checker: it would be cited as evidence.

The contract itself is recorded here so that the M1 change that adds the Patroni image has something
to be checked against:

| # | Contract |
|---|---|
| C1 | The startup path ends in `exec`. After setup, process 1 is Patroni, or a transparent init whose only child is Patroni and which exits when Patroni exits. |
| C2 | No supervisor. No loop that restarts Patroni or PostgreSQL, no supervision suite, no backgrounding followed by a wait. Restarting the container is the kubelet's job. |
| C3 | Signals reach Patroni. A termination signal to process 1 is delivered to Patroni, nothing traps it away, and the container exits within its termination grace period. |
| C4 | A Patroni exit terminates the container, for any exit status, and the container's status is Patroni's. |
| C5 | No PostgreSQL process survives the container. |
| C6 | The startup path never starts PostgreSQL itself. |
| C7 | The probes address Patroni's REST endpoint rather than the instance manager's status port. |

C1 in particular cannot be checked by searching for the word `exec`: it is a statement about the last
statement on every control-flow path, so the M1 checker needs a shell parser rather than a pattern
match. C3, C4 and C5 are statements about a running container and need a container to run.

The M0 substitute is the classification of `pkg/specs.createPostgresContainers` in the inventory above.
That symbol is where the database container's command and probes are chosen, so the audit will report
it the moment the M1 change touches it, and the reviewer is pointed at this contract.

## Known limitations

1. A static audit is not a proof, and specification section 9.3 says so. Reflection, templating, and
   any path through an interface whose implementation is chosen at run time can evade the type-aware
   engine. The mitigation is the chaos suite in M3, not more static analysis.
2. The audit does not scan Patroni. Patroni is Python and lives outside this repository; the
   container contract covers the boundary, and Patroni's own behaviour is upstream's.
3. A baseline keyed by symbol notices a second forbidden call added to an already-listed function
   only through the bucket count, not as a distinct finding. That is the intended sensitivity.
4. The scanner requires the tree to type-check. During a difficult upstream merge it is unavailable
   until the build is fixed, which is reported as exit code 2 so that it is never mistaken for
   compliance.

## Reproduction

```bash
cd hack/cnpatroni/audit

go run . scan                       # print the inventory
go run . check                      # the gate: exit 1 policy, 2 tool, 3 hygiene
go run . baseline --write           # re-record the ratchet, human-invoked only
go run . doc                        # regenerate this document
go test ./...                       # the scanner's own tests
```
